extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of experimental science (physicists, astronomers, chemists, instrument-makers)
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and practical criteria for designing, performing, and evaluating measurements of physical phenomena (choice of methods, instrument design, repetition, indirect measurement, calibration). Useful for experimental scientists and students learning measurement technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ultimate judge must be a sense
rubrics_metrics.description: "By the eye, the ear, or the touch, we judge whether there is a discrepancy or not ... one of the senses must be the ultimate judge of coincidence or non-coincidence."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that at the endpoint of any measurement one sense (possibly via an instrument) determines coincidence; senses may be substituted (e.g., time judged by marks on moving paper). Choose the appropriate sense/index as final arbiter and be aware of conversions between senses (reducing to space magnitudes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Four modes of expressing the measurement equation
rubrics_metrics.description: "This equation may be presented in four forms ... Each of these modes of expressing the same equation corresponds to one mode of effecting a measurement."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the canonical measurement modes (subdivide unit; multiply to unit; repetition; equate submultiples). Selecting the correct mode for the case is a primary design decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: First mode — subdivide the unit
rubrics_metrics.description: When the standard quantity is greater than that to be measured, we often adopt the first mode, and subdivide the unit until we get a magnitude equal to that measured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used for angles (screw and microscope), micrometers (screw micrometer), thermometer scales (division between fixed points). Design instruments to allow fine subdivision of the standard unit for small quantities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second mode — multiply/diminish the quantity to compare with unit
rubrics_metrics.description: "we multiply or divide a magnitude until we get what is equal to the unit, or to some magnitude easily comparable with it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For very small quantities, multiply (lever trains, cog wheels, magnifying mechanical arrangements) without introducing error; for very large/rapid phenomena, diminish them (inclined plane to slow falling bodies, Attwood's machine). Examples: Galileo's inclined plane, thermometric amplifications, Wheatstone's method of drawing off a determinate portion of current.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third mode — Method of Repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: "The Method of Repetition. The ratio of two quantities can be determined with unlimited accuracy, if we can multiply both the object of measurement and the standard unit without error, and then observe what multiple of the one coincides ..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiply both magnitudes until their multiples nearly coincide; if repetition can be extended without increasing absolute error, error per unit can be made arbitrarily small. Best applied to repeatable phenomena (astronomy, pendulums). Includes quantitative argument (error e divided by y). Practical examples: pendulum counts, repeating circle, astronomical long-baseline comparisons. Note limitations: error may be introduced at each observation step if juxtaposition/fixing is imperfect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fourth mode — equate submultiples (rare, less accurate)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The fourth mode of measurement, in which we equate submultiples of two magnitudes, is comparatively seldom employed, because it does not conduce to accuracy."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in photometry (place sources at distances so equal intensities fall on surface; use inverse-square law), Arago's Newton's rings method for equal intensity. Use only when appropriate and with caution due to lower accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use non-invasive optical indices to amplify small motions
rubrics_metrics.description: "Attach a very small mirror to the moving body, and employ a ray of light reflected from the mirror as an index of its movement ... a ray of light is in fact a perfectly weightless finger or index of indefinite length."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For delicate or balanced systems, prefer non-contact indexes (mirror+light, telescopes) that do not disturb the system and that amplify small angular deviations (angular deviation of beam double that of mirror). Examples: Gauss's method, Wollaston's reflecting goniometer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design instruments with tunable sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is a great advantage in some instruments that they can be readily made to manifest a phenomenon in a greater or less degree, by a very slight change in the construction."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make instrument elements adjustable (thermometer bulb/tube size, length/thinness of torsion balance rod and thread) so sensitivity can be increased or decreased as needed. Know which instruments have fixed scale (barometer) and which are tunable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increase sensitivity by mechanical/electrical multiplication
rubrics_metrics.description: "the number of elements or junctions of different metals in the thermopile can be increased so that the tension ... is multiplied; the effect of the current ... can be multiplied ... the excursions of the needle can be increased by rendering it astatic ... the angular divergence can be observed ... by an attached mirror and distant scale."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit amplification at multiple stages: increase number of thermocouple elements, coil turns, magnet arrangements, optical lever arms to convert minute physical effects into measurable signals. Design apparatus as a multi-stage multiplier where appropriate (e.g., thermopile, galvanometers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit natural coincidence and events as measurement aids
rubrics_metrics.description: "Measurements by Natural Coincidence ... a peculiar conjunction of circumstances enables us to dispense more or less with instrumental aids ..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use natural periodicities/conjunctions (Moon showing same face → synchronous rotation; transits of Venus for solar parallax; eclipses and satellite eclipses for angular measurements) to obtain precise measures free from instrument construction errors. Choose natural events that minimize instrumental uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect measurement via related measurable phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: "We need only to discover some other conveniently measurable phenomenon, which is related in a known ratio or according to a known law, however complicated, with that to be measured."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When direct measurement is impractical, measure a correlated quantity and compute target via known laws (e.g., gold leaf thickness from weight + density; wavelength via Newton's rings; ocean depth from seismic/tidal wave velocities; star radial velocity via spectroscope). Ensure theoretical relation is well-established and errors in indirect inference are quantified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit repetition provided by nature for extreme precision
rubrics_metrics.description: "If we can find an observation ... a hundred years ago ... the instrumental errors ... will be divided by about 36,524 days, and rendered excessively small ..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use long time series or naturally repeating processes (earth's rotations, astronomical records) to average down random errors; this is how astronomical constants reach extreme precision. Consider trade-offs: older observations may have larger individual instrumental error; choose optimal time span.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bring experiments into a controllable scale while using repetition for extent
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is always desirable, if possible, to bring an experiment into a small compass, so that it may be well under command, and yet we may often by repetition enjoy at the same time the advantage of extensive trial."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments to maximize control (small apparatus or controlled environment) but use repetition to achieve equivalent large-scale path lengths or durations (e.g., waves in short canal allowed to travel back and forth). Balance control and the need for extensive trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calibrate measuring scales by comparison with the standard
rubrics_metrics.description: "As a general rule, we should not attempt to make the divisions of the measuring scale exact multiples or submultiples of the unit, but ... should determine their values by comparison with the standard itself."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat instrument graduations as arbitrary marks that must be calibrated against a standard; do not assume numeration equals standard units. Perform direct comparisons/calibrations (e.g., transit telescope vertical wires fixed by standard) before trusting scale readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for juxtaposition errors (weights vs lengths)
rubrics_metrics.description: "One reason of the great accuracy of weighing with a good balance is, that weights placed in the same scale are naturally added together without the slightest error. ... the juxtaposition of two metre measures can only be effected with tolerable accuracy ..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose measurement methods mindful that some quantities (masses) juxtapose without appreciable error while others (lengths) suffer significant error when joining segments; invest in microscopes and precautions for length juxtaposition or prefer additive measurements where feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize practical limits of theoretical repetition methods
rubrics_metrics.description: "Theoretically speaking, all error arising from imperfect graduation might thus be indefinitely reduced, being divided by the number of repetitions. In practice, the advantage ... is not found to be very great, probably because a certain error is introduced at each observation in the changing and fixing of the telescopes."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying repetition (e.g., repeating circle), account for systematic or per-observation errors introduced by the measurement procedure (mounting, fixing, observer changes). Evaluate whether repetition actually reduces net error in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of coincidence for comparing periodic oscillators (pendulums)
rubrics_metrics.description: "To ascertain the comparative times of vibration of two pendulums, it is only requisite to swing them one in front of the other, to record by a clock the moment when they coincide ... and then count the number of vibrations until they again come to coincidence."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use coincidence counting (beat/coincidence method) to obtain precise ratios of periods/lengths; count many oscillations to reduce fractional error. Combine with independent clock/electric signals for cross-comparison (as in Airy's experiments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose observation moments to minimize instrumental errors
rubrics_metrics.description: "It will always remain advantageous to choose those moments for observation when instrumental errors enter with the least effect."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select times/conditions (specific conjunctions, eclipses, transit instants) that naturally minimize instrumental sensitivity to error. Planning observation timing is a measurement design decision to improve accuracy.
